Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):,Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,COURSES UNDERTAKEN BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS EMPLOYEES,,The management of Canadian National Railways advises as follows: the company does not maintain records which would show how many employees are registered for a given day.

During the first nine months of 1966, the company paid for the training of 1,095 registered apprentices and 37,123 employees in such areas as Supervisory Development, Sales and Customer Relations and Technical and Skill. In addition, the company pays for various job-related courses and seminars outside the company and under its Educational Financial Assistance Plan reimburses to employees 50 per cent of their tuition fees upon successful completion of approved courses taken at a variety of educational institutions. In this latter case, during the year ended August 31, 1965-the figures for the current year are not as yet available-1,204 employees undertook approved study courses.

Wheat Agreement has been extended to July 31, 1967 pending the negotiation of a comprehensive cereals arrangement which is currently proceeding as part of the Kennedy Round trade negotiations in Geneva. The question of the future of the International Wheat Agreement will be considered by the International Wheat Council during the next few months in the light of developments in the GATT cereals negotiations.

2. and 3. In regard to the GATT cereals negotiations Canadian representation is provided by our Kennedy Round delegation together with other officials, members of the Canadian Wheat Board and representatives of the Advisory Committee to the Canadian Wheat Board as required. Countries now taking part in the GATT cereals negotiations include Canada, the U.S.A., Australia, Argentina, the European Economic Community, Britain, Japan, Switzerland, Norway and Denmark and it is envisaged that other countries will participate at the appropriate time.

column2: Yes. In view of the tactical considerations that are involved and the necessarily confidential nature of the negotiations, specific information regarding the Canadian position on the price issue cannot be provided at this time.
The question of the duration of a new international arrangement covering wheat will be influenced by the other elements. Negotiations have not advanced to a point which permits firm recommendations.

Pearson (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,ITALY-POSSIBILITY OF RENDERING ASSISTANCE,,,Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house, and indeed all Canadians, were shocked by the extent of the disaster which has befallen our friends in Italy. This morning I sent a message to the prime minister of Italy which reads as follows:

Canadians have been shocked and saddened by the news ol the floods in Italy which have occasioned such disastrous loss of life and damage. On behalf of the government and people of Canada, I should like to extend my sincere condolences to you, to the Italian people and particularly to the bereaved.

We have asked for a report from our embassy in Rome as to what form of assistance might be most suitable, and we are also discussing with the Red Cross authorities the manner in which they might join with the government in helping the victims of the terrible disaster that has taken place. I should add that according to our information
November 7, 1966
no Canadians have been involved in the disaster, but we are making further inquiries into that aspect of the matter.

2445845,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.22.2.2,1966-11-07,d25060a9-6d52-4461-a569-fc17c9e6d009,ca.m.654,Mr. Dinsdale:,,INTERIM SUPPLY,,,Mr. Chairman, looking back on the discussion which has taken place during the past week during consideration of interim supply, and particularly after examining the comments of the supporters on the government side of the house, it would be fair to conclude that these hon. gentlemen would like to see the supply debate terminated at the earliest possible moment. Now, I have a very good solution to the dilemma in which they find themselves. I hope they will take the advice which has been given several times from this side during the course of the discussion, as well as the advice which has been given in responsible newspapers across the country, particularly over the week end since the bill to re-organize the Canadian armed forces was tabled and given first reading. Already there has been a spontaneous outcry in the responsible press across the nation to the effect that the course of action recommended by members of the official opposition is the only solution which will make it possible for this house to get on with the important business of the nation.

We have suggested that the subject of defence re-organization, which up until the tabling of the bill on Friday was pretty much an unknown quantity, should be referred to the standing committee on national defence so that we might have the opportunity to hear expert testimony from those who, to an increasing extent in the past weeks and months, have been protesting the course now being taken. As I say, this is a viewpoint expressed forcibly not only by members of the opposition, because we now have been joined in this advocacy in the strongest possible terms by newspaper editorial comment across the nation.

A.s I have indicated, up until the tabling of the bill on Friday, there was a haze of mystery surrounding the intention of the minister with regard to this important subject. No one-and at times I think this would include the minister-seemed to know what specific terms the government had in mind in re-organizing the defence forces. In the initial
November 7, 1966

stages it had been suggested it was a process of integration that would result in a saving of money and an increase in efficiency. There were those who suspected that integration was going to be carried through to unification, and that the Canadian armed forces were going to be transformed from a defence force to a glorified international peace force. The bill has confirmed our worst fears in this regard.

When the minister has participated in the course of the debate he has indicated that his position has been crystal clear, right from the very beginning of his tour of duty as the minister of defence. Even though I have not been a member of the committee, both inside and outside the house, I have endeavoured to follow the ministerial meanderings. I must confess that I have received a more clear-cut idea of what the minister had in mind from his statements outside the house than from those he has made in the house.

In order to indicate that there has been a haze of misunderstanding and lack of information on this subject, I am going to quote no less an authority than Mr. Blair Fraser, writing on this subject in Maclean's magazine as far back as January 25, 1964 under the heading ""Can an ex-private bring common sense to our defence policy?"" This indicates, I believe, that the minister did not have the foggiest notion where we were heading on defence policy. On page 37 of that issue Mr. Fraser made the following statement:

Final decisions on the size and type of Canada's ground forces will be part of the decisions about Canadian armed services in general. These will be more closely co-ordinated, less independently concluded by army, navy and air force. The decisions themselves will be determined by the role that will be more precisely defined in future than it has been in the past.

Integration of the services doesn't have to mean that any of the traditional services will be abolished, or that all servicemen must wear the same uniform. All that's likely is the establishment of a clear, common chain of command, with common services (supplies, accounting, procurement, etc.) when they can reduce costs or increase efficiency. The effect on efficiency is expected to be greater than the effect on costs-few people who have studied the structure of defence think integration will make it much cheaper, but they do think it would become a lot more efficient.
That was a statement by Mr. Blair Fraser when the minister first announced his policy. This statement is along lines parallel to the sentiments which have been expressed on this side of the house.
Interim Supply

It is quite obvious that during the past two years the minister has gone much further than he himself originally contemplated in the reorganization of Canada's armed forces. I think he has been pushed over the precipice by the strength and influence of his own press releases, because it must be admitted that until quite recently press commentary with respect to this drastic, major overhaul, has been largely of a laudatory nature.

I have indicated that it has been in speeches made outside the House of Commons that the minister has revealed his real intent. Last July it was my privilege to attend the meetings of the Air Force Association held in Edmonton, at which the minister was guest speaker. He clearly set forth there, in fact more clearly than we have heard it expressed in the House of Commons, the ultimate purposes he had in mind. He pointed out that he had consulted with his advisers that they had come to the conclusion that there would not be any nuclear war in the future, and that therefore Canada did not have to make any provision in that regard. He said, further that after consulting with his advisers they had reached the conclusion that neither would there be a conventional war in the future. And, speaking of advisers, it is remarkable that many of the minister's advisers have either resigned or been prematurely retired, and recently have been protesting quite vigorously against the minister's policy.

He also said that what we would have to contend with in the future was a series of brush-fire operations, and that this is what the government of Canada was gearing Canadian forces to meet. Now we know, and this has been substantiated in the bill introduced last week, that our national defence program has been reduced to a peace-keeping force that might be described in terms of an international R.C.M.P., integrated, unified, and so carefully streamlined that it will remove forever Canada's position of influence as a world force in determining world affairs. It is little wonder that over the week end editorial comment has strongly protested against this procedure.

During the course of this debate on unification over the past two years I have often wondered about the motivation of the minister in trying to turn back the clock by one half century in the matter of Canada's defence policy. This is exactly what he is trying to do: He is trying to go back to a period some 50 years ago when we had a
November 7, 1966
Interim Supply

unified force. At that time we had no navy and no air force. Our armed services were unified, largely because we were regarded as an insignificant power in world affairs. It was only over the course of the past 50 years emerging out of Canada's gradual development, and her growing position in world affairs, we achieved a defence policy which makes it possible to maintain our sovereignty and be listened to with respect in the councils of the nations.

For example, in world war I and world war II the Canadian navy established a reputation and built up traditions that are second to none. It was only within the past quarter century that our air force established a similar enviable reputation among the defence forces of the world. Now the minister is reversing that policy, and blandly says that his is a new concept in military policy which is going to produce the most efficient, the most envied, well organized and effective fighting force of any nation in the world, and that within a decade or so every other nation will be following Canada's good example.

The minister further says that though there have been temporary set-backs, as has already been pointed out today in matters of morale and recruitment, these will be short lived, and once the people of Canada and the members of the armed forces understand what the government is trying to do, they will flock to the colours in unprecedented numbers. This reminds me of the supreme optimist who said, ""Today things are average. It is true things are worse this year, but they will be worse next year."" This is what we can anticipate from the policy announced by the minister in the bill which he introduced last Friday.

Why is the government taking this step? Some have suggested that it is part of the continuing campaign that goes on among government frontbenchers with respect to personal advancement and consideration in the leadership race. I am not going into that argument. It has been covered substantially during the course of this debate, but certainly the unseemly haste in proceeding with this matter and the stubborn refusal to allow the defence committee to make a thorough review of it, would suggest that there is a rigid timetable involved, with events to culminate about the middle of centennial year, 1967.
Others have suggested that it is the result of personal pique because the minister had an unhappy experience during his own service career. There was confusion between the

armed forces, with the result that he received double inoculations and that sort of thing because the services did not compare medical notes. Some have said that it is because of this personal experience that the process of rigid unification is being pressed. If this is so I would remind the minister that that problem has already been resolved because the medical corps is now integrated, in line with the sensible and reasonable policy of integration established under Hon. George Pearkes. Integration is what we thought was in the government's mind when it first started on this course to avoid duplication in the purchasing service, the medical corps, the recruiting service, and so forth; but now we know that with respect to national sovereignty and the armed services, we are going backwards 50 years.

I do not see how anyone who served operationally in either world war, and particularly in world war II, could become obsessed and preoccupied with the subject of unification according to the terms as set out in the bill now before the house. We found that the best type of unification took place during world war II when it became necessary to move forward as a combined force. Speaking from the air force standpoint, I recall that we were organized into airfields, and air crew were trained in infantry combat techniques. In addition to being trained in multiple military skills we also had the incentive to maintain our own unit identification, our national identification, and that spirit of healthy competition and rivalry which is basic to the maintenance of morale in the armed forces.

This is the best kind of unification. Anyone who has had combat experience must appreciate that if you try to destroy the traditions of unit designations, if you try to put everyone in the same common mould, if you try to destroy the heritage of the Canadian armed forces that has grown up over the past 50 years, then in effect you are doing precisely what that great number of former advisers to the minster have been warning us about since their resignations and premature firings -you are destroying the ability of the Canadian forces to maintain their obligation as a national defence force. So I would say that if there is any personal pique involved in this matter, let us set it aside and think in terms of the welfare of Canada.
Some say that there is a republican motivation behind this move; that this is one way of
November 7, 1966

getting rid of the symbols of our military and political heritage, namely, by erasing and eliminating the structure that has developed slowly over the years and in this fashion start again from scratch. The authority for this particular viewpoint is, of course, Mr. Terence Robertson, who over the past few years has been quite close to the Prime Minister in these matters, and professes to be quoting the desire of the Prime Minister with respect to our armed forces.

But there is another reason, and this has not been discussed very much in the House of Commons. I would say that this is typical Liberal philosophy toward Canada's defence program. We have only to go back to preworld war II to realize the situation that existed on the eve of that world war. We have only to go back to the immediate postworld war II period to realize that Canada reduced its armed forces to such an extent that when Korea came along in the early 1950's we had to resort to a crash program. During those days Hon. Brooke Claxton was our minister of national defence. This was at the time I first came into the house. Hon. Brooke Claxton was constantly under fire because the government had destroyed the ability of our armed forces to meet any defence obligation which might arise in the sort of world in which we were then living. Indeed, the situation in which we are living now is even more serious, and threatening. We had to build up our armed forces suddenly from scratch. I would say that the defence mess that resulted in the early 1950's was largely a result of the typical Liberal approach to Canada's defence.

When the minister came into office he said there was a mess in the Department of National Defence. If there was any mess it was due to the period of scurrying about in the early 1950's trying to make amends for policy reversals which took place at the end of world war II, which were much the same as some of the policy decisions which appear to be motivating the bill that is now before us. The first attempt to bring order out of chaos came about in 1957, when the long lived Liberal administration was replaced by a Conservative administration. Then, the Hon. George Pearkes, the first minister of national defence under the Conservatives, started an integration program which was designed to bring about over a reasonable period of time, the savings in tax dollars and the efficiency about which the minister first talked when he vaguely referred to integration. These two
Interim Supply
objectives will be destroyed if he goes through with the unification program contemplated.

I have already indicated to the minister and the government that if they want to get on with the business of the house, if they want to close this interim supply debate, all they have to do-and it is their decision to make-is accept the reasonable request that has come from members of the New Democratic Party, members of this party and is now being re-echoed across the country. I refer to the request that a matter as important as this, one involving the sovereignty of Canada and our ability to meet our defence obligations including our obligations and commitments under NATO and the United Nations organization, should go immediately to the defence committee. We in this party can assure the minister that our most knowledgeable members on defence will be seconded to that committee. The minister claims that the committee has had an opportunity to discuss defence matters comprehensively and thoroughly.

I have not been a member of the defence committee and I was amazed, when I considered the developments from outside the committee, that there had not been a protest long before from some of our permanent force people. It seemed passing strange to me that, when the government was proceeding with a policy that we conjecture will destroy our defence integrity, those men in the upper echelon of the three branches of the service should remain quiet. But now there are 40 such men available to give expert advice on the matter. They are available to give the expert advice that obviously the minister ignored at, I would say, the peril of the country. I am not speaking of the peril of the government, because the minister might be able to bamboozle the people of Canada by an attack on the brass, those men who have given distinguished service to Canada over the years, who have served a life time, some of them in two world wars and whose advice has been completely ignored.

These men are now being derided by the Minister of National Defence as hidebound Colonel Blimps. For my money, Mr. Chairman, I would much rather take the advice of these distinguished servicemen designated by the Minister of National Defence as Colonel Blimps than the group of men he now seems to have around him as advisers. They are obviously not advising on defence policy; they have been chosen for their positions because
November 7, 1966
Interim Supply
they are willing to serve as apologists for the government.

This debate has been going on in the house for several months, and it will go on with increasing force across the country. 1 suggest that it would be in the best interests of Canada if we took this discussion out of the arena of partisan politics and personal and party ambitions. We should have a face to face confrontation of members of this house from all parties and the men who resigned in protest, but who seem willing now to bring the information to the attention of the people of Canada, through the instrumentality of the defence committee.

The minister has been attempting to deal with the decline in our armed forces in various ways. He has, for example, increased the rates of pay to the armed forces, which is to be desired if it is followed by other necessary measures. But I am sure that members on all sides of the house will agree that the strength of Canada's defence policy has been, not necessarily in the permanent force men but in the citizen basis of the armed forces.

The voluntary support of our citizens has made it possible for Canada to play an important role in the two world wars of the twentieth century. One cannot inspire cooperation, support and patriotism by depending on a mercenary approach to service to one's country. While it is true that a little bit of sugar makes the medicine go down in the long run and in the kind of world in which we live today, it is the support of the citizens' army and of volunteers, such as we have had in the past, which will determine whether Canada has a force adequate to meet her international obligations.

Mr. Chairman, there is another matter which has been mentioned in the course of this debate, that is the future function of our committee system. During the past few months we have made some worthwhile breakthroughs in parliamentary committees. As has been said on several occasions during the course of this discussion, if the minister, in the face of a growing appeal from all across the country, declines to give the members of this house and the people of Canada who are vitally interested in defence matters the opportunity to use the broadened scope of our parliamentary committee system, I am afraid that the new, noble experiment will expire before it really becomes alive.

This subject is too important to become bogged down in a partisan rough and tumble in this House of Commons. It should be above and beyond the ambitions of any one man, particularly of the Minister of National Defence. As we move forward in this discussion, there is only one matter to be decided and one point to be assured, that is that Canada's armed forces will continue to play a strong role as a part of Canadian foreign policy and as a most vital aspect of our maintenance of national sovereignty.

I agree with an increasing number of people in the country who believe that the minister's bill is going to set back our progress in this regard by some 50 years. I plead with him, while there is still opportunity, to refer this matter to the committee on defence. He has indicated he will do so after second reading of the bill. We all know that after second reading the principle has been established, and discussion of this bill in committee can only be a rearguard action. Now is the proper time to do it. We have other important matters to come before the house, and there is no necessity for unseemly haste.

Integration of the healthy variety has been proceeding at a proper pace. If we proceed to unification now we will reduce the Canadian armed forces to the position in which they were during the years immediately following world war II. I am sure the minister, who was in the House of Commons in the early 1950's will agree that that would be a disaster to be avoided at any cost.

2445846,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.22.2.3,1966-11-07,6ab1d342-3030-459c-9751-639f09fada02,ca.m.6516,Mr. Salisman:,,INTERIM SUPPLY,,,Mr. Chairman, I should like to use the few minutes at my disposal today to discuss the proposed route of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines through the United States. It is my opinion, and the opinion of the party I represent, that the government's decision to approve Trans-Canada's application for this route will be a step that Canada will have every reason to regret. This is one further step along the route to continentalism. I presume most Canadians have not had an opportunity to make their decision as to whether or not our economy should be integrated with that of the United States. Since this opportunity has not been provided, I hope the government will not take steps to preclude such a decision. This government does not have a mandate to create a continental economy. I hope they will recognize this fact, and withhold the application, because certainly this is the crux of the matter. The government is not the only one that has taken us
November 7, 1966

down this path. The much heralded national oil policy, which was brought in by the Conservative government when they were in power and was supposed to be an answer to all our problems, has not worked to the advantage of Canada.

Certainly, it has corrected some minor deficiencies and to some extent it has increased the production of oil in the west. But I would submit that we could have done a great deal better had we then decided to build a pipe line to Montreal, instead of allowing the oil companies to decide the way in which our oil was going to be marketed in this country and all around the world. It is certainly true that the national oil policy was not based on a decision of the government but on the decision of the oil companies who wrote it and suggested it to the government of the day. The national oil policy has helped no one except the international oil cartel of the world which has decided on the allocation of markets and we have fought for them every inch of the way in order to get sufficient exports. This policy has not achieved the purpose for which it was created at that time. I think it can be pointed out that the members of my party supported the policy. I suggest that had they been able to foresee the development of that policy, they would certainly not have supported it at the beginning. We are not prepared to do so today.

There are also indications from members of the other political parties-although they are hesitant about saying so-that the national oil policy is in serious need of review. I think we should not just review the policy. We should abandon it and create a new policy which will ensure that all Canadian oil needs are met from Canadian production. Some of the studies that have been made indicate that such a policy is feasible.

The United States automotive agreement is another instance of a situation into which we have drifted. We are now in a position where even those who do not want to see an integrated auto industry between Canada and the United States have no choice in the matter. We are therefore faced with a continental automobile policy. And now we are being asked to endorse a continental gas policy. Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the time has come,
Interim Supply
if we are genuinely concerned about retaining the differences between our country and our neighbour to the south, to say no; it has gone far enough.

We could not halt the drift to a continental policy when the national oil policy was introduced. We probably could not halt the drift to a continental policy in automobiles. I submit, however, that we certainly can halt this drift today to an integrated gas policy, and this is what we should do.

I really cannot understand how we have placed ourselves in this position. I watched the minister when members of the opposition made speeches in favour of his policy. Nor do I think he has any reason to take very much satisfaction in view of what has happened. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister, who I think is a genuine nationalist, has been sold out. I think he has been sold down the river. Military Engineering, an establishment which has made a great contribution in the field of engineering in the past and which is capable of continuing to do so in the future. 2445897,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.22.2.54,1966-11-07,5e00ed8a-3ebd-48a2-9a20-ce869b0c9ca8,ca.m.9673,Mr. Pugh:,,INTERIM SUPPLY,,,According to the Minister of National Defence, the real issue before us is whether or not the integration of our armed forces is the right policy for Canada to follow. Those are his words as reported in Hansard on page 9353. It is all very well for the minister to say that. He is telling us that this is the only issue at stake. But I find myself more in agreement with the statement 23033-609
Interim Supply
which was made by the hon. member for Greenwood as set forth in Hansard at page 9354.

At the moment, however, I should like to deal with what I think is the main issue. I should like to join with and support the protest already raised by members of the official opposition against the continued and obstinate refusal of the Minister of National Defence and the government he represents to allow the committee on national defence to review adequately the merits of the unification proposals-before parliament is asked to give its approval in principle on second reading.

If there is a difference of opinion, we must assess its effect on parliament. I suggest that this effect is twofold. At the present time an exceedingly dangerous situation is forming slowly and there is no question but that in the very near future it is going to come to a head. The first of these two main facets is that supply must be granted. Unless supply is granted, of course, the whole machinery of government may well come to a standstill. The second facet is consideration of the main estimates before the house.

I do not think we should overlook this most important point about the granting of supply, because unless money is voted in the next few days many, many departments are going to suffer. In respect of the estimates, there is perhaps a very important point indeed; that is, by the rules of this house we now are limited to 30 days, which includes this debate. If this debate continues for 30 days, then when is the government going to examine the expenditures of the other departments? The government may say, ""well, 30 days; you simply could not think about going on for 30 days"". I suggest to them that they carried the debate on interim supply for 26 days while they asked many questions to which they wanted answers.

Because of the importance of this whole defence proposition which is before us today, I see no reason for the debate not continuing. I am suggesting at the moment that it will continue, but the government has the solution to this problem by referring this subject and all of its ramifications to the standing committee on national defence. I think it is very important that they think about this. It is not good enough to say, ""well, what is the difference between sending it to the committee before second reading and sending it to the committee after second reading"".

I am quite sure most of us are for integration and that we would agree to the principle of the bill. But anyone who has been a member of this house for any length of time knows that on other occasions when a bill has been sent to a committee after second reading there has been little, if any, change made. Certainly, no change asked by the opposition ever has been made. If we were to vote for the bill on second reading and then try to have it changed later in committee, such efforts would be a nullity. I do not wish to stress too much the fact that our rules call for 30 days, and 30 days only, to cover all the estimates including interim supply. But I must tell the government that when we agreed to the 30 day restriction everyone here did so in the utmost good faith and with the object that the committees, including the standing committees, would consider in full the various estimates of the department and anything else which might happen to come up. If we are to be denied this procedure because of this debate, what a laughing stock this government will become-and I do not mean parliament-when they finally arrive at the 19th hour of the 30th day and say, ""come on, pass the estimates of these departments; the rules say we must"".

This absurdity lies right in the government's lap, and is one which must be cleared up. There is another thing, of course. The opposition must examine government expenditures and must examine them in detail. This is a time honoured precedent. If suddenly we are to be faced with a whole group of departmental estimates at the 11th hour, then we cannot give them a proper examination. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, and I hope the government listens, that this is a situation which should not be allowed to develop in parliament.

Many words have been spoken about the committee system, particularly in respect of the standing committee on national defence. I have many volumes here from which I could quote, but perhaps it is not necessary. I think it is necessary, however, to reiterate what has been said in this debate from time to time; that is, the committee system has been in vogue for a long time. However, since this government took over the committee system has become something new and different. The whole idea in respect of the committee system, and particularly the committee on national defence, was that we should have full access to facts. I might, of course, go back to a statement made prior to the election, on
fMr. Pugh.]
March 26, 1963, by the Prime Minister when he was speaking in Kingston. This reference is particularly to the defence committee:

A Liberal government also would set up an allparty commons defence committee right away to take the defence issue away from partisan politics. The committee's work would be part of a Liberal government review of Canadian defence policy to determine an appropriate role for this country. Such changes also would ""take considerable time"".

Those are the words of the Prime Minister, and I do not think he has changed his views. If one were to examine the views he has expressed in this house with regard to the setting up of committees, one would find no difference. The essence of what he has said is that there will be a full examination of the facts. This is a good objective, and is what committees should do. Committees should work; they must work, because if they are used properly they save the time of the house-the very case in point today. We have a standing committee on national defence, and it should meet to hear all the arguments before second reading of the bill. I will return to this point later.

This matter should be examined by a committee, so that we do not waste the time of the house. The government tells us it has plenty of business with which to proceed. Why then does the minister not send this whole subject to the standing committee on national defence, so that the government can proceed with this other business which members of the government claim is so important? When we give the okay to the estimates of each department we are saying, ""okay, go ahead and spend the money"". We cannot be rubberstamps; we must examine these estimates in detail.

What is being requested in this debate? We are asking that a more thorough examination of defence matters take place, and that the minister's bill be sent to the defence committee prior to second reading. It will be too late to send it there after second reading because the committee could talk from now to doomsday and the government would not change the bill in any respect. The last occasion on which we had such a bill before the committee, the government introduced its own amendments but accepted none from the opposition parties.

It is useless for the government to say that full consideration was given to unification by the special committee on defence. This is something which was stated by the associate minister and by government supporters. The
November 7, 1966

minister himself has said, ""I gave you full disclosure; I gave you every opportunity. The witnesses who were called before you stated their case, and no questions were asked. What are you objecting to?"" We are objecting to the fact that evidence was tampered with, and this is something which has come out since the last meeting of the committee. This is, if you like, new evidence. Obviously members of the committee were led astray by the evidence which they received from competent witnesses, because that evidence was tampered with. It would have been much better had those witnesses not been called at all.

The principle of uberrima fides, which means the utmost of good faith, is involved, and this principle has been violated in no uncertain terms. A witness who had prepared a brief had the essence of his brief changed. What was given to the parliamentary committee was a watered down version of the facts. The witness may have given his evidence in good faith. He did not complain. This is part of the duty of a serviceman but he, along with many other servicemen, thought it of sufficient importance to say, ""We wish to protest"". In fact, there has been a rising tide of protest since the committee last met.

Once again, I say it is useless for either of the ministers to say that we had a chance in committee and did not use it. I am not saying that the evidence was designed to mislead, but from talking to members who sat on the committee I can say there is no question but that it did mislead. It gave a wrong impression and there was bad faith involved. I repeat that such witnesses should never have been called or. if there were any changes made in their evidence, that evidence should have borne a note reading, ""This evidence is being given after having been vetted by the Minister of National Defence."" It could then be given its true value.
Our purpose is to get to the facts, and in this connection I should like to quote what the minister said when he was in opposition, as recorded at page 2214 of Hansard for March 18, 1960:

Why should the minister not answer policy matters in committee? He has to do so in this house when there is a debate on national defence matters; he has to do so in committee of the whole house when his estimates are before us. Why is it any different with respect to answering policy matters before a special select committee? As a matter of fact the atmosphere there is more conducive to a non-partisan discussion; the mere physical appointments are more conducive to intelligent, easy study of very important and far-reaching problems. In addition, there the minister 23033-6091

can allow his officials, if he wishes to do so, to make direct answers to questions. This speeds up the proceedings

I suggest that there was no change in the minister's attitude when he reached the glorious position of being Minister of National Defence. As recorded at page 483 of Hansard for May 30, 1963, he stated:

I felt that, in order to have an intelligent discussion in the House of Commons, and through the House of Commons, in the press of the country, a great deal more information would have to be made available, and a much more detailed examination of the facts would have to take place by a committee especially set up to spend a lot of time and energy on the study of that information.

I think at the outset of its deliberations it should seek-and this of course will be up to the committee itself-briefings on the most fundamental of facts, and bring forward the body of information on which a more comprehensive discussion, including policy discussion, can take place.

The minister now asks, what more do you want? He says, go ahead; get the facts. Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not think we can get the truth from tampered evidence, and this is what the committee had before it. It was on this evidence that the committee made its decision. But having made its decision, a lot of people in the services came forward and told us, ""I did not mean that. I was restricted by the minister in saying what I wanted to say, and what I should have said to the committee"". This comes back to the principle of the utmost of good faith, and anybody who fights against that principle should not be in the House of Commons. How can brainwashed evidence be considered proper evidence to put before a committee of the house?
Again quoting from the minister as recorded at page 9345 of Hansard for October 31, 1966, I read these words:
The Prime Minister and I felt, however, on the basis of our experience in opposition, that the lack of such a committee-
He was trying to pour oil on the waters.

-meant that inadequate information on defence matters was available to members of parliament and, through their deliberations, to the Canadian people. We felt that the quality of debate would be improved and that the background information required for intelligent discussion of defence matters warranted the establishment of a defence committee, notwithstanding the historical objections.
What clearer statement could be made. Contrast this statement with his later statement: ""Well, you can have witnesses all right,
November 7, 1966
Interim Supply
but before they say one word to you either I or my department are going to tell them exactly what they are going to say.""

Opposition members feel that the evidence given to the defence committee was tampered with, and it resulted in the committee reaching a conclusion that was not in accordance with the facts. I think it would not be a bad idea to look closely at the speech made by the Associate Minister of National Defence. I sat in the house last Tuesday night and listened to him very carefully, because I respect him. I listened to every word he said, and I have read his speech over and over again. The reason I mention the speech of the associate minister is that he spoke with great sincerity. He told the house that after listening to the speeches of hon. members he wanted to resolve the doubts in his own mind. There is no question about this; one has only to consider the words of the associate minister as reported at page 9393 of Hansard. At the outset of his speech the associate minister said:

I agree with most speakers on the other side of the house who stated that it was an extremely important matter which should normally arouse public opinion and on which it is difficult to have a well-grounded opinion.

I, myself, wanted to make up my own mind, to come to my own conclusions, since I am not a military man-

I give the associate minister full credit for that; he wanted to find out for himself, as do members in all parts of the house. I include government members because they must be asking themselves: What is this Minister of National Defence trying to do?

closely connected on this question. The associate minister said:
I, myself, wanted to make up my own mind, to come to my own conclusions, since I am not a military man, and to convince myself that this was a worthwhile endeavour.
What did I do? I called upon people in the trade, which is recommended by the hon. members opposite-

The whole of the associate minister's speech should be read by all members of the house because he is a man of integrity, and I do not believe for one moment that he would try to hoodwink the house or put anything over hon. members.

If the associate minister was able to satisfy his conscience, surely all hon. members are entitled to have their consciences satisfied by being able to examine witnesses and not by having to accept hearsay evidence. This is of paramount importance at the present time, for the reasons I have given, and it is all the
November 7, 1966

opposition asks. Because of the very serious doubts which have arisen in this regard, we want to resolve this question. I have no worries on the matter because I feel sure the associate minister will bear in mind those points I have brought out. 2445917,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.23.3.1.3,1966-11-07,f8c074be-3032-4ab6-af4f-11618169c92a,ca.m.8084,Mr. Coates:,,INTERIM SUPPLY,SITTING SUSPENDED,SITTING RESUMED,Mr. Chairman, the storm signals have been raised in the Atlantic provinces, and one of the means of endeavouring to determine the extent of the dangers and pitfalls is through interim supply. The Minister of National Defence has been less than candid in his statements on the future policy of his department and the government in so far as national defence is concerned. Because of the importance of our future national defence policy and because of the future problems which the Atlantic provinces will of necessity face if there are cutbacks and consolidations, it is the endeavour of members from the Atlantic provinces, particularly those in the Progressive Conservative party, to try to determine as best we can exactly what we will have to face in the days ahead in order to overcome any difficulties that may develop if the government's national defence policy continues to erode morale in the services and fosters the continuous disappearance of personnel from all three arms of the service.
The Minister of National Defence has been both stubborn and arrogant in his attitude toward the house. He has not relented in his

stubbornness even though such newspapers as the Winnipeg Free Press, which has always been one of the main spokesmen for Liberal thinking in this nation, has told him and his party to send the unification bill to a committee before second reading so that full consideration and discussion may be available to all members of parliament and, indeed, to the country, on what our future defence policy should be. It is indeed a strangely difficult and tortuous road that the Minister of National Defence has started upon, and as he marches down that road he will find that many obstacles will be in his way if he continues the philosophy he has pursued to date.

As I have said, Mr. Chairman, we in Atlantic Canada have great fears about the attitude of the minister toward the future defence policy of this country. Many statements have been made about the changing role of Canada in international affairs and the significant effect it will have upon our defence policy. The minister chooses, however, to allow Canadians to remain in the dark even though statements by intelligent and knowledgeable people have indicated a very significant change in thinking on the part of the government as far as national defence is concerned.

There is a great deal of talk about a significant reduction in the size of our armed forces. There is talk of a change that will mean the breaking of our obligations to NATO and NORAD. There is talk about changes whereby Canada will adopt a peacekeeping role in association with the United Nations and that this will be the only role for our defence forces in the future.

There has been no statement by the government that this may be their intention for the future, but in view of the fact that these statements have been made and that the government continues to remain silent on such matters, one comes to the fearful conclusion, that this thinking may well be in evidence among cabinet members today. It may be, of course, that such thinking is only in the mind of the Minister of National Defence. It may even be that his attitude is paramount to that of the other members of the cabinet, that in his own mind he has reached the position that he can challenge his leader and cabinet colleagues and force them to march down the road to international irresponsibility whether they like it or not,
November 7, 1966
threatening that he will resign his position if he is intimidated in any way so far as his own ideas are concerned.

These conclusions may not be correct, Mr. Chairman. However, we are not in a position to do anything but arrive at such assumptions in view of the lack of communication that exists between the minister and the members of this house. If parliament does not have the rightful responsibility to learn from the minister exactly what are the government's intentions, then I do not know who has. Surely the minister cannot lead parliament around blindfolded in the hope of getting whatever he wants so far as a national defence policy and a national defence force are concerned.

What concerns me even more, is that in Atlantic Canada for many years much of our economic stability has been based on what the armed forces provide by way of federal money. It may be foolhardy to think that we should continue to expect this kind of stability of employment and income from the defence dollar, but I see no reason why we should not. It is my belief that as a growing nation with increasing responsibilities we have a growing commitment to the international community to take a greater role in national and international affairs, including the defence of this nation and assisting our allies to defend the free world.

The fact that the 1963 election campaign was fought on the basis of whether or not the government of that day had broken an international commitment to accept nuclear weapons would lead one to believe that this government would be a little more concerned about its international commitments so far as national defence is concerned than about any other subject. Yet what do we find in this regard? We find a degree of demoralization, particularly in the navy, that has placed that arm of our armed services in the position where it can no longer meet the commitments of this country to NATO. What does the minister say about this? He ignores it. He sloughs it off, he laughs about it.

This is the same minister who was so critical of the Conservative government in 1962 which he said was breaking one of its commitments to NATO. It is a strange individual that we have today as Minister of National Defence. He is a frightening man. In his arrogance and his silence he endangers not only the economic advancement of the Atlantic area but Canada's international
Interim Supply
reputation and our image abroad. He does not allow our nation to maintain its responsibilities in international affairs.

He goes to Halifax to have an eyeball to eyeball meeting with the servicemen, to talk frankly to them and to be spoken to frankly. One can almost imagine that he would want the press of this nation to pass on to the people what a forthright and able individual he was in this frank discussion. One would think, with the minister being so sure in his mind that the majority of people in and out of the services were in full agreement with his defence policy, that he would be anxious for everybody in Canada to know how acceptable and how right was his course.

He went to Halifax. He had his eyeball to eyeball meeting with the servicemen, without benefit of the press. What happened, Mr. Chairman? He was hooted at. He came away from this eyeball to eyeball meeting and when people said to him, ""We understand you were heckled"", he said, ""If I was, I didn't hear it."" If he did not hear the heckling he must have used earplugs. Everyone in the services who attended the meetings heard it. Those people made it evident, and are making it evident every day, how unhappy they are with the defence policy the minister is trying to shove down the throats of the Canadian people. Men are leaving the services. Today, answering a question-and this may be a side issue-the minister said that men are leaving the services because there is so much prosperity in this nation that they can make more money elsewhere.

Everybody knows that today Canada has one of the most highly paid defence forces in the world. There is job security. Ability has merited advancement, or it did until the minister started his unification program. The minister's explanation will not be accepted as the reason for the tremendous exodus from the armed services in evidence today. The men are leaving because morale is low, because they are unhappy with the government and what the government has done with the national defence policy of this nation. They are unhappy with what the government plans for the future and are afraid that Canada will break all its international commitments in a determined effort to make Canada a neutral nation. Neutrality means that we will allow the United States to defend us. It cannot mean anything else. It means that we shall go on our merry way as

a peace-loving people unwilling to accept our responsibilities under our international commitments but willing to have approximately

column2: men available for brush-fire wars threatening the peace of the world.

column1: How sad it will be for this nation if the minister is allowed to continue in an arrogant manner to impose on the Canadian people, without discussion or debate, a national defence policy that he has conceived without regard for parliament, his Prime Minister or his party. And they are all afraid of him over there. They let him go on his merry way unchecked, just as they let parliament go on debating interim supply, knowing full well that we shall soon reach the end of the line, the point of no return, if the people working for this nation are to be paid.

All this reminds me of the manner in which we got into the most damaging debate that has taken place in this chamber since I have been here. I am talking of the flag debate. At that time the government ignored the facts of life and the priorities of action in this nation. The government was determined to produce a flag and impose it on the Canadian people. They imposed it without regard for their responsibilities as a government running a nation. They showed no responsibility to the people of Canada in the legislation they imposed. They were determined to impose their will on parliament and the people.

Here we have the same sort of situation. Here we have legislation that cuts into the heritage and tradition that are so much a part of this nation. It cuts into them or cuts them out-""cuts them out"" is the better phrase, I think. The government is not the least interested in associating Her Majesty or the word ""Royal"" with our armed forces, no matter how long that word has been embedded in our national way of life. This is a strange government doing strange things for strange reasons.

The hon. member for Grey-Bruce has risen in the house on at least 50 occasions to ask the government house leader when we will debate old age security. What happened? We were told that unification was more important to the government and to the Minister of National Defence than old age security and that the unification bill would take priority over the needs of the old age pensioners. That was not the story the people were told in the election campaign of 1965. Indeed, in those days nothing revolutionary was men-
tioned in regard to national defence policy. It is amazing, once this government received its mandate, how it changed its priorities to suit itself, not keeping faith with the voters of this nation.

This has happened in two election campaigns. Indeed, if there were another election campaign and the government were elected again, which is a very slim possibility and getting slimmer every day, it would be the same story again. It is becoming a repeat performance of the 22 years when we were cursed by governments led by a number of Liberal prime ministers, though mainly by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King. We are getting back to those days, and nowhere is it more evident than in the Atlantic provinces where for 22 years there was broken promise after broken promise until the people of the Atlantic area had to march to Ottawa and onward to find employment to provide the sustenance of life.

We do not intend to do that again. We intend to stay home and fight for the things we have a right to expect from any government. In my constituency there is an aircraft plant which has provided employment for a great many years. The company has been laying off men left and right. I asked the Minister of Industry the other day in the house what he proposed to do about it. He told me he knew nothing about it. His officials knew about it but he did not know about it, and probably he did not care a devil of a lot. It is just one of the facts of life that when the Grits get in we go down. There is little hope for the Atlantic area with a Grit government in power in Ottawa, and this has always been the case.

I do not know what lies in store for us as far as national defence policy is concerned. A number of contradictory statements have been made about the future of the bases in the Atlantic area. The minister has given us an assurance that our fears are unnecessary. But the same minister gave a similar assurance to my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria about the Point Edward naval base, and the words were hardly out of his mouth before the base closed down.

Let me tell the minister that the people who look to the base at Cornwallis for economic survival are not depending on his word today. They are banding together in a nonpolitical force and they intend to exert every possible pressure available to them to make the public aware of what will happen to their area if the minister proceeds to close the base, as they expect he will, in 1968.

The great problem facing members of the opposition is that they cannot talk reason to this minister. They cannot convince him that if his policy is as acceptable to the Canadian people as he believes it to be, he would probably get his wish and get his unified force if he would agree to provide the hearing for which we are asking. But what we are sceptical about is the extent of the support the minister really has. There is good reason for this scepticism. The minister appears to be afraid to allow public discussion to take place in the defence committee. It is one thing to be reasonable. It is another to try to make reason prevail with a minister such as the one now holding the portfolio of defence. Silence and arrogance, a complete disregard for parliament, are more in accord with his way of life than the reason evidenced by this party during recent days when we have urged the hon. gentleman to provide full information not only as to our present defence policy but as to our future role so far as national defence and our international commitments are concerned. Short of closure being introduced, the hon. gentleman can rest assured that until he relents, until he listens to reason, he will continue to face questions of the kind I have been asking tonight. If he wishes to jeopardize the pay of the people who are employed by the federal government, that is his responsibility, not ours.

Let this bill go to the committee before second reading-

2445922,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.23.3.1.8,1966-11-07,50d4b628-2609-4c79-99ff-0a8add8715e9,ca.m.1327,Mr. Scott (Danforth):,,INTERIM SUPPLY,SITTING SUSPENDED,SITTING RESUMED,-and let a full hearing be held. I hope that what happened here this afternoon has not escaped the attention of the house. Both the hon. member for Okanagan Boundax'y and the hon. member for Cumberland have again made clear that the official opposition takes such a serious view of the minister's position and feels that this matter is so vital and fundamental to our whole concept of military defence and the institution of parliament that they intend to withhold supply until their grievance is answered and some action taken upon it. I do not know what view the government will take, but it is fairly clear to me that if the official opposition persist in their view-as is their traditional right-we in this group have done it too on occasion-then we are headed into the type of debate which will make the flag debate look like an afternoon's discussion. It seems to me that this is what the minister is bringing upon both parliament and the government which supports him.

If the proposition is that the defence policy of the government-integration, unification, amalgamation, or whatever it is-is to be examined, then now is the time to do it and not after we have frozen ourselves into the same difficult and almost hopeless position we found ourselves in during the flag debate when neither side would give in and the result, on reflection, was one which was undesirable, unnecessary and unworthy of us. None of us came out of the flag debate with any glory. Let us not have another flag debate over the military policy of the government at this time. The government is in control, not those in the opposition, and if the government does this it will be doing to its legislative program now what it did during the flag debate. It will be sabotaging and rendering futile its own legislative program. The flag came from nowhere. We had been given a long list of important legislation and then out of nowhere came the flag and it was pushed through to the conclusion. We know what happened. Almost all the legislative program went down the drain then. It seems to me this is the position that the government and the minister are going to place us in again. We will not get medicare this session. We will never get to the old age pension legislation.

2445932,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.23.3.1.18,1966-11-07,50d4b628-2609-4c79-99ff-0a8add8715e9,ca.m.1327,Mr. Scoff (Danforfh):,,INTERIM SUPPLY,SITTING SUSPENDED,SITTING RESUMED,There is another matter about which I should like to say a few words and put something on the record because there are some questions which we should like one of the other ministers, who is unable to be with us tonight no doubt for a perfectly good reason, to answer. I wish to say a few words about the Canada-United States auto agreement. The statements made
November 7, 1966

last week by the Minister of Labour made clear, if we ever had any doubt, that the whole U.S. auto agreement has become a complete fraud on the public. Those of us who have followed the agreement from its beginning have always been highly dubious about it. To us it was originated in haste and secrecy and passed by excutive order. We were not even permitted to review it until it had been in force for 15 months. We have always expressed grave doubts about it and we now find that the whole thing has been an exercise in virtual futility.

I will refer to two aspects of the matter which I should like to put on the record, and I hope the Minister of Labour will answer. I have in mind what has happened with regard to the rights of the workers and, second, the rights of the public with regard to prices. One member of the opposition, the hon. member for Wellington South, no doubt will deal with the business aspect because he is more conversant with it than I.

I want to go back to the origination of this agreement. It was an agreement whereby the government by its own action brought in certain tariff charges which everybody admitted would cause dislocation in the automobile industry, but we were assured by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Industry that the workers in this industry would not suffer any hardship as a result of government trade policies.

We were told that the government would bring in a scheme called transitional assistance benefits, TAB for short, and that under the legislation a fund would be set up to which the government and the industry would both make contributions, with the money being used to assist the workers should they become unemployed as a result of the trade agreement. At that time we expressed great doubt about the wisdom of such an agreement unless it were mandatory for the automobile companies to participate, but we were assured by the Minister of Labour that we need have no worry, that the motor companies were waiting anxiously in Windsor for the agreement to be signed and then they would hasten to deposit their cheque for $50 million. As events have transpired we have now found that the motor companies never participated in the agreement and that fewer than a dozen workers received benefits under it up until last summer. As a result, that aspect of the agreement
Interim Supply
has become a complete sell-out by the government.

There is another side to the story. In their agreements the automobile workers over the years have negotiated for what are called supplementary unemployment benefits or, in short, SUB. These benefits are in the nature of wages. They are fringe benefits paid into a fund which was to be used to compensate the auto workers during periods of model changes, which are normal lay-off periods. It was never intended that these benefits be used for government purposes.

But last week we found out from the Minister of Labour that the government has released the motor companies from their obligation to participate in the plan. We found out that the government is going to use the taxpayers' money to pick up the difference, that the workers are going to be forced to use up their own wages in the form of fringe benefits and that once these fringe benefits have all been used up the government will then start making the so-called TAB payments to them.

This is the biggest sell-out I have seen since I became a member of this house. Over the last two years the government has, cynically and coldly, completely sold out to the automobile manufacturers, and I warn the government that we are not going to let this go until we get some sort of explanation as to how it all came about. The government in effect has almost stolen the workers' SUB payments and has done what it said it would not do when it told us that under the agreement the workers would not be forced to pay the price of change, that because the community was forcing this upon them the community would pay, and that the motor companies would be in a position to contribute and help.

The government told us that under this agreement the motor companies would receive a bonanza of $50 million in the form of rebated duties and duties they would not have to pay. This was to be an annual gift for three years, and I can remember the Minister of Labour standing up in the house and giving us the most solemn undertaking that the motor companies were going to be forced to make their fair contribution to the scheme to assist the workers. Now this has all gone down the drain; the motor companies are off the hook. But the workers are being forced to give up their SUB benefits, and only when they have been exhausted will the government pay the TAB benefits. It is a pretty
November 7, 1966
Interim Supply
shoddy, shameful story of performance by a supposedly good government. I only hope the minister can give an explanation for this sad, sad story.

But again we have been sold out; there has been no reduction in prices. Instead, there has been an increase in prices wrapped up in a very skilfull explanation about safety features.
