2445935,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.23.3.1.21,1966-11-07,f52b315d-220a-46b9-903a-008063ef0fd1,ca.m.7825,Mr. Nugent:,,INTERIM SUPPLY,SITTING SUSPENDED,SITTING RESUMED,Mr. Chairman, I believe that the tone set by the previous speaker is one I should and will try to follow, a tone of reason, logic and common sense, which I am sure many of us like to feel is basic to any intelligent discussion of the problems before the committee.

I believe the hon. member was very kind to members of this party in pointing out how calmly logical and reasonable was their approach to the question of defence. Certainly he did credit to that argument by the manner in which he presented it, and the same could have been said the other night about his colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood. Anyone who listened carefully to those speeches, and who believes it is his duty in this house to give due consideration to common sense when it is heard, must have been impressed. Personally, Mr. Chairman, I have never heard a better exposition of the present defence situation than was given today by the hon. member for Queens. It was a very concise and complete review, something that all of us are trying to achieve in the present darkness that surrounds us.

I want to sum up the situation as I see it. The minister is strenuously, and I think that word is chosen advisedly, resisting any suggestion that the members of the House of Commons should have the benefit of a searching re-examination of all the facts pertaining to defence before we proceed further to deliver his unification baby I am completely puzzled, as I am sure most hon. members are, by the position he takes. Not for one moment do we imagine that the minister, by acceding to our perfectly reasonable requests for a further study of the facts, would in any way be admitting that his policy is not correct. In fact, I think it could not in any way be taken as a sign of weakness of faith in this policy. On the contrary, as was just said by the hon. member for Danforth, and it has been mentioned previously in the house any refusal to re-examine the facts can only be taken as indicating fear in the mind of the minister that such an examination so earnestly desired by this house would weaken rather than bolster his position.
I believe that the words of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary were very well chosen when he referred to the speech made
November 7. 1966

by the Associate Minister of National Defence. The hon. member said that the associate minister mentioned that he was troubled because the subject was so important and complex that he had to be sure in his own mind he was proceeding on the right course, that his conscience could not be satisfied other than by a re-examination of the facts and by seeking the advice of those he thought were more learned in the profession, shall we say, of defence than himself.

I would say, and I hope this will not be taken as derogatory of the minister, that I would not be satisfied with the same advice that the associate minister received. I feel he is too close to the Minister of National Defence. We have learned much too much about what has gone on in the armed forces to believe that the sources of information available to the associate minister would be other than the carefully winnowed opinions of those left in the armed forces who agree with the minister or those who have been fortunate enough to be able to hide their disagreement so far to keep from being fired. While I am sure it is incumbent upon the associate minister to give his fellow minister the benefit of the doubt and to have faith in that advice which the minister says is so important-after all, it is the advice that the minister ordered them to give him-we can be forgiven for suggesting that we want a little better than this.

I am suggesting that the associate minister has certainly captured the conscience of every member in the house by the position he has taken. I cannot imagine the Minister of National Defence asking any member of his or any party in the house to do less than follow the example of the associate minister, who showed us so clearly what is the duty of a conscientious member of this house. That duty is to search his conscience very carefully to satisfy himself that he has obtained all the evidence and advice enabling him to understand that evidence, so that he may well and truly come to the position where he is satisfied that what the government is doing in this most important area is correct.

The white paper on defence says that integration is a first step toward unification. I think this matter was explained very well by the hon. member for Queens. It is a first step, and if approval was ever given to the white paper that approval was given only to the first step. As the Minister of National Defence has explained, unification is such a radical departure from pure integration, which has
Interim. Supply
been tried to a varying degree by armed forces all over the world, that it must be understood that the next step toward unification is a very large one.

In this regard I disagree with the associate minister, who said that unification was a natural extension of the theory of integration. I find that I have to agree, no matter how seldom this may occur, with the Minister of National Defence in this regard, namely, that it is a bold, new, entirely different step and therefore requires us to pause carefully and find out what we can before proceeding with it. It has been asked: Is integration complete? The evidence is that we have not finished experimenting with integration. We are not satisfied that it has been working properly. There is no evidence before us that can make us so happy with all the experiments that have been tried along this line that we have confidence in proceeding further.

I think the house has in a way been sadly misled by the minister's approach to this problem. Certainly it is a source of great gratification to me that so many of the newspapers are commenting in such a critical fashion, saying that they understand so well the cry that goes up from opposition members in this house, and agreeing that an examination by the defence committee after approval in principle of the bill sounds rather silly. The duty of members of this house is to vote when they have been informed as to the facts and have satisfied their conscience.

I admit that if we cannot do that there is much to be said for the apparent position of the minister when he says: I have perfect confidence in this action. Give the bill second reading, then call the committee and you will find that I have been right. You can then examine to your heart's content and be reassured. The only trouble is that this is a most deceitful sort of step to take. Second reading of a bill gives it approval in principle, and anyone who has any acquaintance with the rules of the house knows very well that once the house has decided on the principle it would be impossible for the defence committee to bring forward any evidence about that principle. Unification would be a fact, and all those witnesses who warned the minister so solemnly of the dangers of his policy and were fired for their pains could not be called before the defence committee because we would then be trying to examine what the house had decided and it would be contrary to the rules. Before that committee we would
November 7, 1966
Interim Supply

not be able to discuss the principle of unification because the house would have already decided it. Therefore what the minister is saying is not: Pass this bill in principle and then look at it. He is saying: Pass this bill in principle so that you will never be able to look at it.

I think we had better understand that, because while there may be much to be said for the opinion that at least the minister has taken an honest stand and he would be open to great criticism if we examined this matter before giving the bill second reading and would be subject to condemnation which would be most embarrassing, that is not the position at all. Instead of the open attitude that we will be able to look fully at the facts, with the minister having to stand up to the censure of public opinion and of members of the house as a result of that full examination, the simple fact is that if we follow the advice of the minister and let him do what he wants parliament will be refused any chance whatsoever to look at the facts of unification, to hear any opinions on unification or even to discuss the subject. This is somewhat different from the picture the minister has presented to us.

Without doing the minister an unkindness, in my view it is entirely consistent with the attitude he has shown in this house as minister that he should say that all this house requires is the solemn assurance of this self-styled expert that, on the advice of those who have remained after he has fired all those who do not agree with him, he is satisfied we are on the right course and that parliament should now, despite the warning of the Associate Minister of National Defence that we have a duty to satisfy our conscience and to make sure we are voting correctly, accept the minister's words and assurance. The minister asks us to do that in spite of the fact that we lack adequate information which has been desperately hidden up to this time. He knows that by passing this bill in principle we bar forever any possibility of re-examination until the taxpayers become so impatient at spending so much money for so little that public opinion will again somehow force the matter upon the attention of parliament and of the government.
This argument seems to me a little inconsistent with what was said by the minister, that great champion of the rights of parliament, when he was a private member. Let
the committee consider the contrast. I read from page 9346 of Hansard of Monday, October 31. The minister quoted Robert MacGregor Dawson as saying the following:
-and he therefore has the power to overrule any of his civil servants at any time.
Farther down the page the minister said:
It is fundamental to our parliamentary practice that the minister responsible for a department will have the sole discretion as to the limits of the special material that his officers may present.
As we can see, the minister makes it clear that not just special material but any facts will be under the sole discretion of the minister and that parliament may receive that and no more.

The most powerful advocate I can find to argue on behalf of members on this side of the house against the minister's approach to this problem is the hon. member for Trinity. It seems to me that even more beloved to him than the advice of those top-flight officers whom he has promoted because they have so valiantly echoed his advice would be the advice of the minister himself as he gave it to this house and to the then minister of national defence when he was but a poor backbencher struggling to provide members of parliament with the knowledge which is indispensable to them if they are to do their duty in the house. Listen to some of these gems. I now quote from page 5378 of Hansard of the session of 1959, volume 5. These are words which I am sure the minister will recognize as his own. He said:
To try to hide from this parliament and the Canadian people the state of its confusion and lack of policy the government has clamped down what I call a rigid insecurity blackout.

I certainly admit that nowhere is there a suggestion that when Mr. Pearkes was minister of national defence he went so far as to tamper with evidence to keep the facts from the public, but at least the feeling that all the evidence was not available was enough to warrant that sort of speech from the present Minister of National Defence at a time when he was a private member.
As found on page 5379, toward the bottom of the left-hand column, he said:

It is true the minister himself and the deputy minister did make themselves available, for which members of the delegation were very grateful indeed; but of course the minister and the deputy minister only gave members of the delegation such information as would, they thought, not be embarrassing to the government here and certainly not sufficient to prepare us to deal with and talk intelligently to the members of the United States delegation.
November 7, 1966

I am sure this will have a familiar ring to the minister and will convince him of my argument. I trust no one will accuse the minister of being insincere when he made those remarks or of being inconsistent because the remarks which he made as a private member contradict those which he is now making as the minister. Perhaps the consistency is in the insincerity at both times.

I hope he will not mind if I quote a few more phrases from that source of advice and wisdom which I have never known the minister to ignore, namely, himself, and in fact the source of advice and wisdom which, so far as we have been able to determine, is the only one that carries any weight with him. I trust the committee will bear with me while I give the minister another small reminder of how serious these matters are to the backbencher. Again on page 5379 the minister said:

Furthermore, the Minister of National Defence has consistently and repeatedly refused to give serious answers to the questions asked in the House of Commons. He has given the house and the Canadian people the impression that either he himself is not fully informed on defence matters, or that parliament and the Canadian people who are asked to foot the bill have no right to sufficient information to be able to judge the merits of the government's proposals.

Mr. Chairman, those are very stirring words, and I submit they were not spoken at a time when the government of the day was embarking on a venture not only unique in Canadian history but throughout the whole western world. They were not uttered at a time such as now when we have every reason to believe that this action, having been studied by the defence forces, has been rejected year in and year out and when we know that so many top military advisers have rejected it because it is not sound. I am sure that the words of the minister, who as I said, is his own best adviser, will be taken to heart by him.
Farther down on page 5379 there are more stirring lines which really appeal to me as I am sure they will appeal to the minister and the Associate Minister of National Defence. He said:
The government may not want parliament and the Canadian people to know, but we have every right to know-

I perceive from the look on the faces of some of the blind followers of the minister on the Liberal side of the house that they are not really interested in hearing the sage advice of the Minister of National Defence spoken at a time when he was a backbencher.
Interim Supply

I gather they realize that it is only since he became a minister that he has acquired the super knowledge which alone can justify the turning down of all the best technical advice on defence in the country. I am not sure in what other way I can impress on them the seriousness of the situation, but I think there is one thing which they do recognize and that is our striving for the right of parliament to have all the information.

The only reason I can find for lack of concern on their part is that their concern for their party's history of bungling is such that they would sacrifice even the rights of parliament to protect whatever tattered image they may still retain. Perhaps my method of appeal should be simply to point out that the public is getting wise to the minister. The glow on the halo has dulled to some extent. The bland assurances which have gone over so well for so long a time are finally starting to tarnish in the light of common sense and the dogged determination on the part of members of this house to ensure that until there is some valid reason given why parliament cannot have information we must continue to seek it.

Sometimes the minister seems to be almost hurt by our unwillingness to accept the assurances which he gives us every day. I have pointed out tonight one difficulty. His assurance that if the defence committee is reconstituted the bill will be sent to it after second reading with no limitation placed on the questions asked is, of course, pure nonsense. The minister does not have that authority no matter how supreme or superior to parliament he may think he is. This house is governed by its rules and they are very simple. Once we approve of unification in principle, then lost forever is any opportunity to question the principle or to examine the factors behind it to see whether it is right or wrong.

Again, Mr. Chairman, the question before the house is not whether it will be of any benefit to us to examine this principle after it has been declared, but that we should be given the knowledge to enable us to decide whether it is possible to implement the principle. Therefore the stand taken by the minister is not that we give approval in principle and then examine the bill but that the house is not entitled to this information. As I say, once we give approval in principle we will never be able to look for this information.

Interim Supply

I started out by saying that our position is a simple one. It does not involve the minister in making any concession or yielding any point. All it involves is the admission that the associate minister was speaking very truthfully-indeed, he caught the conscience of every member of the house-when he said that we must look at the facts and satisfy ourselves as to those facts.

It is true that it might be a little embarrassing for the minister, this factor having taken so long to get through to him, if he were finally to decide that common sense shall prevail and that he will do for this house what we would have been the first to scream for were he on this side, namely, let us have the facts. But I submit that it is better to be swayed by argument and to yield to common sense than to let it become ever more apparent day by day that the only thing that stands in the way of a rightful examination of the facts is a stubborn refusal born of fear of what those facts will reveal.

This minister, I submit, has been able to sell the people of this country a bill of fare which indicates they are going to get more defence for less dollars. It seems the minister's view is that it is better that this concept should begin to wear a little thin, to have the people of this country and the newspaper editors seriously question it, than to go before a committee and prove it. I suggest that we must continue to press the minister on this point no matter how embarrassing it is to him, that we must continue to argue from the most logical basis our approach to this problem. No man convinced of his stand, so beleaguered as the minister and so confident as the minister says he is of his policies, would so stubbornly refuse to reveal the facts. You and I know, Mr. Chairman, that in any argument we are ready, willing and anxious to prove our case when we have put it forward honestly. I submit that if the minister has any faith in his argument he must do this too.

I am sure that the members of this house will recall the flag debate, which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Danforth. After a very bitter and acrimonious struggle for several weeks, finally the Prime Minister was persuaded of a very simple and logical position which had been taken on this side of the house from the start, namely, that it is not just what you want to do but the manner in which you do it that can be so important. On that occasion the Prime Minister finally sent the flag question to a committee for consideration. We had asked him to do that

from the start on the simple basis that it was in a committee that the subject could best be handled. If we were going to change our national flag it was much better that we should start out in a co-operative and common sense endeavour than to have the acrimonious debate that resulted, which divided the people and turned the flag not into a symbol for the future but only a bitter remembrance of the stubborn determination of the government to do in the wrong way what they thought was right.

It is surely not unreasonable, Mr. Chairman, for the members of this house to remind the government that if we are to have a new defence policy the people of the country are entitled to test it. People are entitled to security. Any new defence concept must be tried and tested by their representatives and must have the confidence of the members of the House of Commons behind it. It must be a policy which is based on a thorough, searching examination of the facts. Even though it may be new and experimental it must be subjected to test and receive the seal of approval of conscientious men who have diligently tried to make sure that it is the best possible concept of defence to adopt.

The people of this country are entitled to defence and to have confidence in their defence policy. This can only be achieved by a common-sense and close examination of the facts. Therefore I would ask the minister to indicate that he is not afraid of the facts by consenting to send this question to the defence committee for examination before approval in principle.

However, defence matters set aside, I would like to speak tonight in defence of certain problems which farmers have to face and about a pipe line which would provide them with better income.

I would like to refer to the visit which the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) made to Quebec on October 19, where he attended the C.F.U. provincial convention. Some federal members from Quebec had the privilege of listening to the interesting speech which the hon. minister delivered to the delegates. As pointed out by the president of the Quebec C.F.U., it was the first time a federal Minister of Agriculture attended their convention. At the very start of my remarks, I should like to quote two paragraphs from the minister's address, as follows:

Most of the territories cleared by the early French settlers were divided into what appears today to be small farms or simple pieces of land. In those days, the farm procured the necessary food, shelter, and often clothing. The members of the family provided the labour and, since the operation yielded virtually everything necessary, the family did not need much cash to purchase the Items needed for its subsistence and for the operation of the farm.

It is very difficult to compete but we are doing our best under the circumstances. Frankly, I think we have done fairly well in view of the very real competition which exists at the present time. It has been frequently suggested that the present manpower shortage is evidence of the low morale owing to the implementation of the integration program. The particularly healthy state of the Canadian economy has resulted in an unprecedented demand for highly skilled, highly trained personnel and the ability of the civilian economy to pay larger salaries than is possible in the armed forces.

Hon. members are well aware that the recruiting and re-enlistment of the armed forces have always been directly related to the strength of the economy. United Kingdom and the United States, which are experiencing similar economic conditions, have also been affected by manpower shortages.

In January of this year the national board for prices and incomes in a report to the parliament of the United Kingdom noted that the British armed forces had had an over-all shortfall of 18 per cent in their recruiting target. The report went on to say:
In short, the services are facing a formidable problem in recruiting and retaining sufficient personnel and in their view (the services) the problem is likely to grow in the next few years.

Manpower shortages have and will no doubt continue to affect the maritime elements of the forces to a far greater extent than either the land or air arms of the service. This is understandable to a certain extent in view of the environmental factors of long tours of sea duty and prolonged separation from home and family. Again, however, this is not a factor that can be related to integration, nor is it a problem that is unique to Canada.

On March 14, 1965, the New York Times reported that of the service men in the United States navy only one-fifth of those eligible were re-enlisting, and in addition primary recruiting had dropped drastically. In comparison, recruiting and re-engagement rates for the Canadian forces reflect a healthy state of affairs.

We have not been content, however, to allow the present situation to continue. Major steps have been taken to bring pay, allowances, housing and other factors in line with life in the civilian economy, and we will continue to make improvements in the future as they are required. However, I repeat that there is no evidence to support the contention that recruiting and re-engagement rates are related to the policy of integration and unification. Our naval re-engagement rates are better than those of the United States or the United Kingdom. I am sure that no one would suggest that the reason the rates of the United States and the United Kingdom are so low is that they are not unifying their forces. Certainly I would not make such a suggestion.

2445968,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.23.3.1.54,1966-11-07,6ffdccf5-fe20-4be5-b99d-1593863458ac,ca.m.1985,Mr. Hellyer:,Minister of National Defence,INTERIM SUPPLY,SITTING SUSPENDED,SITTING RESUMED,The policy was clearly set out in the white paper. We stated that the best way to meet any demand for United Nations assistance would be from highly trained, well-equipped conventional forces, forces with sufficient flexibility to contribute to the deterrence of major war at one end of the spectrum and peace-keeping operations at the other end.

In a relatively short time, just a few years, we have greatly increased our fire power to the point where it is greater than ever before in our peacetime history, we have substantially increased our mobility by air and sea, and we have provided our servicemen with a broad range of equipment to permit them to carry out this wide variety of missions. We plan to continue to expand our capabilities in all these areas.

Another allegation is that we are moving too quickly, that we are carrying out the program without due thought and consideration. In my opinion we are not. The initial planning of the integration to unification process began over three years ago, in 1963. One year later the white paper was issued outlining the pattern we would follow. The paper came as a result of months of concentrated study.

The white paper itself set out our long-range objectives and goals. In order for the program to be effective it has been and is being subjected to the closest scrutiny. Every area is being researched to determine the best method of implementing the changes. It is a very complex process covering all aspects of training, supply, finance, organization, logistics and all that which goes into the makeup of a military force.

Because of this unification, assuming the legislation is passed this fall, will not become a total reality until approximately 1970 or 1971 when all the planning and implementation are completed. Thus the whole process will have taken about seven or eight years.

2445989,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.23.3.1.75,1966-11-07,acd5380d-f564-427d-821a-4528ecdba8f3,ca.m.9577,Mr. Gregoire:,,INTERIM SUPPLY,SITTING SUSPENDED,SITTING RESUMED,Yes, that is exactly what I told you. I shall be attending the committee tomorrow, Wednesday and Thursday-it is not good when the house and committees are sitting at the same time-and I cannot be here. I have to make my speech tonight.

Mr. Chairman, the debate on interim supply has been going on for approximately eight days and I have not yet had the chance to say a single word. Now, you will admit, notwithstanding the reaction of my hon. friends here, that it is quite exceptional for me not to be heard, not to speak eight days in a row in the House of Commons.

Therefore, I hope the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) will bear me no grudge, since he was granted every possible opportunity for eight days, at least I never interfered, not having said a single word for the past eight days. And the hon. member for Grey-Bruce will admit that this is quite remarkable. And it is one of the reasons why I feel I must take advantage of this opportunity, even though, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to speak on defence matters. I think we heard about it these last days and I would now like to deal with a matter in which the Canadian people, the taxpayers, are interested.
We have been seeing in newspapers, for the last two or three weeks, advertisements concerning Canada savings bonds, the so-called centennial series Canada savings bonds.
One thing makes me wonder. It is said concerning this centennial series:
Invest now and double your money in twelve years.
It is said in the advertisement for these savings bonds:
Your money will double In twelve years.
November 7, 1966

Well, Mr. Chairman, this means that if an individual's savings will double in twelve years, inevitably, Canada's debt will double in the same period. What Canada, what the government borrows today, it must repay double in twelve years, and yet, the Canadian citizen will have received only one dollar and Canada, that is the government, will have received one dollar only, but in 12 years from now, it will have to repay two. Since the person investing in savings bonds will receive in 12 years from now two dollars for each dollar invested, that means that the government of Canada, for each dollar received, will have to repay two in 12 years. That is why Canada's debt will have doubled within 12 years, and the country will not be getting anything in return. The same amount will be spent once and repaid twice. If $100, $1,000 or $1,000,000 are borrowed under this Canada savings bonds issue, in order to build the Department of National Defence building now under construction, well the building will have cost $1 million, but $2 million will be repaid. An amount twice the cost involved will have to be reimbursed.

Mr. Chairman, you will admit nevertheless that it is a strange system when the government of a country, which is supposed to be an autonomous and independent government, is compelled to repay twice the cost. Every government expenditure is repaid twice, and this is confirmed by the advertisements for Canada savings bonds which read:
Your savings will double in value in twelve years if you lend to the Canadian government.
Those who lend $1 will get $2 and, therefore, if the Canadian government borrows $1, it will have to repay $2.

But the inconsistency of all this goes even further. When it is time to repay, those who have loaned money to the government will be taxed in order to be repaid, because after all, the government must find the money somewhere in order to repay the Canada savings bonds at double their value at the end of 12 years. Where will the government find the money? Well', under the present system it must tax the Canadian citizens and those who invest in Canada savings bonds do not realize what they are doing. They are lending Canada $1 so that Canada will repay them $2, but the Canadian government will have to levy a $3 tax in order to repay them $2, because there are then all the debt charges, all the inspectors, the bureaucrats, the civil servants, the government accountants, etc. Therefore,
Interim Supply

the government is doing some work for $1, it must repay $2 and tax those persons who have made some savings and invested them, in order to reimburse them. How will it be useful for a Canadian taxpayer to invest $100 in Canada savings bonds, if the same Canadian citizen is taxed two or three times in order that the capital and interests may be repaid?
Now, one realizes that such a system is very beneficial to the Canadian taxpayer. He lends money and he is required to give three times more to be repaid.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether those who buy savings bonds known as Canada centennial series issue, are making a good investment. People invest money in such a fund and afterwards taxes are levied to pay them back and one is taxed more than what one has loaned and more than one is supposed to get back.

Such savings plans, Mr. Chairman, which are called savings plans, are nothing else but plans to get Canada into debt and plans to increase taxes to repay Canada's debts. It is a strange system, because it is also a system where Canadian citizens, when they have savings, are asked not to invest them in the country's assets or development but in its debts. Those savings bonds are used to get the country deeper into debt, to increase the country's debt twofold, instead of only once, since twice as much than what has been received once is paid back, and the Canadian citizen will invest in the country's debt what he can save on his salary, on his profits. And when the time comes to develop our natural wealth, when the time comes to develop our secondary industries, when the time comes to develop our primary industry, Canadians no longer have any money. They have money to invest in the country's debt, but when the time comes to develop what would really increase the country's wealth, to develop our natural resources, they have no money, since all their savings went into the country's debt, the government's debt.

And that happens twice, because those savings are used once to be invested in Canada's debt and then people will be taxed a second time to repay those debts. It means that our savings go into the country's debt twice. And the debt increases twofold, since the government pays back twice what it borrowed.
And when the time comes to develop our natural wealth, the citizens of Canada have no more money. They are broke, they have no money in their pockets, everything has gone
November 7, 1966
Interim Supply

for the country's debt and there is no more to develop our natural resources. And what happens? Well, then, to develop our mines or forests, our streams, because our savings have been used up, because the government has taken our savings, we wait until some Americans, Englishmen or foreigners come to invest their own savings in the development of our natural resources.

That, Mr. Chairman, is the strange development system we have in Canada. Our own savings are used to get us into debt and to get the Canadian government into debt, and when the time comes to develop our natural resources and our industries, there is no money left and foreigners come to develop our wealth, our natural resources, our industries and they own all that and get the profits and dividends. And we remain stuck with the country's debt and with the taxes needed to pay back the public debt and the interest on it.

And our Canadian citizens play that game, because the government goes in for a lot of advertising about the Canada savings bonds. And I say it again: those advertisements say: ""Invest a dollar and get two back."" Lend the government a dollar, in 12 years, you will get two back. But if the government pays back two dollars in 12 years, it means that our debt has doubled in 12 years. And the savings of the Canadian citizen are buried in the public debt; we have no money left, and foreign people are coming to develop our country.

And today we wake up, we are loaded with debts, we have invested all our money into the public debt; we owe about $22 billion but our industry is not our own, our natural resources, are not our own, they all belong to the extent of 78 per cent, to foreign people, because they have used their savings to develop our country while we have used ours to increase the public debt. And when you increase the public debt, the government is forced to increase the taxes to pay back the interest on that debt. And this year only, the government is going to tax the people to repay $1,280,000,000 in interest on our debt. And those who have bought savings bonds will be taxed so that they may receive their interest. If the Canadian people could realize what kind of game is being played, I think that they would invest their money better.
I think that it would be advisable to find a better means to finance the development of our country. I see that the Minister of
Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) who is in charge of Expo '67 is here tonight.

I think he does not have his earpiece on at the moment. If somebody would draw his attention, I would have a question for him at this stage. Further to the preliminary remarks I have just made, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

I was saying that the Canadian government is forced to borrow, through savings bonds, to finance its undertakings. I understand that the Expo in Montreal-and that is what I wish to inquire about from the minister- that Expo '67 has put bonds on the market to finance its undertakings. I also understood that such bonds had been purchased by the Bank of Canada and that it was not necessary to borrow from foreign sources or from chartered banks. It means then, that the Bank of Canada has financed that public undertaking known as Expo '67. If that is so, if that is a fact, so much the better.

I should then like to ask the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce-perhaps he can answer later-if it is true that the bonds issued by Expo '67 have all, or at least, for the greater part, been bought by the Bank of Canada, so that in fact one gigantic public development was financed not by debts but by the Bank of Canada?

I hope that some time in the course of the debate on interim supply now before the house, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce will find the opportunity to answer that question, namely whether the Bank of Canada financed, pending returns, as great an undertaking as Expo '67.

Even then, that is better than financing the party the way the Liberals do, with the help of big financiers and fat campaign funds. There is haggling in Quebec these days over election funds. Some say: Do not reveal the sources of revenue, because then people will not want to contribute once they know who has already paid into the Liberal campaign funds. This cannot be divulged, because it would then become apparent that those who run things are the big financiers who contribute to the Liberal election fund. A case
November 7, 1966
column2: COMMONS

column1: in point is the fact that a candidate running for president of the Quebec Liberal Federation has stated that ever since the question of divulging the sources of contributions to the Liberal party election fund came up, contributions have dwindled. It is frightening. Some do not want any part of this, others want to contribute on the sly, so that nobody could link them with any political patronage.

The Postmaster General knows it exists within the Liberal party, he knows it for a fact. Well, in our case, we contribute, we build up our fund thanks to the good people who, like the minister said earlier, want to buy pens which will enable us to write out the independence of Quebec, and before long.

I shall continue, Mr. Chairman, after this interruption by the hon. Postmaster General, who could however deal with his own employees and see to it that there is no strike within the Post Office Department.

Mr. Chairman, I think that if the Bank of Canada can finance such a huge concern as Expo '67, there is no reason why the Bank of Canada or a national bank-in independent Quebec, we say the Bank of Quebec-should not be able to finance all public works, whether it be a subway, roads, bridges, schools, universities or hospitals. The national bank should finance these public works, so that the government will not always have to take the savings of the people, leaving them without money to invest in Canadian industry, in Quebec industry, Quebec trade, or the natural resources of Quebec or Canada in order to develop the country. The national bank should finance all these public projects and private capital should remain in the hands of private citizens, so that they can themselves finance the industrial development, the commercial development and that of the natural resources of their country, without having to ask foreigners for capital.

2446001,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.26.1,1966-11-07,adda36bc-8669-4e53-b76d-1081337ec422,ca.m.2331,Mrs. Grace Maclnnis (Vancouver-Kings-way):,,HOUSING-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN BUILDING RECREATIONAL FACILITIES,,,Mr. Speaker, a week ago I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), under whose jurisdiction the National Housing Act comes, whether he had received representations from the city of Vancouver asking for an amendment to the National Housing Act which would permit federal help to be given for the building of recreational facilities in public housing projects. My question was not in the correct form and therefore I am raising the matter again now.

This is a very serious matter and one which has caused much concern over quite a long period to social workers, civic officials, elected representatives and responsible citizens in all walks of life, so much so that the Vancouver city council, which is not noted for making up its mind hastily in these matters, in September decided that it would provide one-third of the necessary money to build recreational areas in its four low-rental housing projects if Victoria and Ottawa each

column2: COMMONS

column1: Proceedings on Adjournment Motion would pay one third also. The federal Minister of Labour said that such assistance is not permitted under the National Housing Act. Therefore, on October 25 the Vancouver city council decided to send the mayor and a senior alderman to Ottawa to meet the Minister of Labour in November to press for an amendment to the National Housing Act which would permit this to be done. Two days later the Minister of Labour introduced into this house his proposed amendments to the National Housing Act. X have looked over these very carefully and there is not a word concerning any provision for federal aid to build recreational facilities in these public housing projects.

For a moment or two I should like to discuss the need for these facilities in the four low-rental housing projects in Vancouver. As I say, there is a great and growing public concern about this matter. In order to give the house some idea about the need I will take one example from some of the material in a brief which was prepared by the Skeena Terrace Tenants' Association. Skeena Terrace is one of the low-rental housing projects in Vancouver in the riding of my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). Perhaps more than any other this project is illustrative of the need to have these homes made into real genuine homes for tenants instead of boxes for beds which is the case in a good many of these housing projects right now.

The reason for the need for recreational facilities, above all, is that there is a tremendous density of people in a very small land area. Skeena Terrace would cover about three city blocks. I think it houses over 800 people of all ages, including nearly 600 children. I know Skeena Terrace well. It is located in a hillside with very steep land gradations. There just is no place outside that is suitable for children's games and there are no proper facilities inside for recreation. On the north, south and east Skeena Terrace is bounded by heavy industrial projects.

On the north and west boundaries there is only a very short distance between Skeena Terrace and exceptionally heavy traffic arteries. In effect this has made an island of the area, with no green or flat space on which children can play. It has isolated the people in this area and remember, Mr. Speaker, they are low income people. There is a heavy concentration of children in the area and a large number of elderly people as well.
DEBATES
column2: November 7, 1966

column1: The trouble is that the two existing community recreational facilities in that part of the city are situated too far from Skeena Terrace for the children to use. For the majority of tenants on low income the cost of transportation to existing facilities, especially for families with several children, is prohibitive. In addition to membership cost at the community centres, many programs have fees attached to them and familites on limited incomes find this a heavy burden.

The closest park facility has to be reached by crossing a main traffic artery. Indoor facilities there are negligible and the grounds are used by organized teams, so that children who reach it from Skeena Terrace sometimes cannot use it. Added to this is the problem of the senior citizens who have difficulty in getting access to the community grounds.

The Vancouver board of parks and public recreation did supply one full-time recreational director during part of the summer months but was forced to remove her as there were no satisfactory areas in which she could work with the children. Local housing authority officials are handicapped because they are not allowed any money for expenditure on recreational facilities.

The tenants themselves have tried through their own efforts to get help from private organizations. Alexandra neighbourhood services association has supplied them with a qualified worker for two days a week, and the Company of Young Canadians recently sent them two fine young people to work there full time. However, there is not even office space, let alone recreational space, in which these people can work.

I suggest that before it is too late the minister should consider adding this type of amendment to his proposals to amend the National Housing Act. People living in commercial housing and apartment buildings enjoy games rooms and party rooms. They have terraces and swimming pools. If these things are desirable for people living in the cramped space of commercial housing and apartments, then surely they are necessary for the tenants of public housing.

The delinquency rate in the Skeena Terrace housing project has been remarkably low so far, but I have talked to social workers who are afraid of what will happen to these children when they grow older and do not have adequate facilities to keep them busy. At present they are completely cut off from
November 7, 1966

the games and recreational facilities they should have. There is no use talking about waging a war on poverty if we do not provide recreational space for people in such projects, and so I urge the government to consider providing the necessary money.

Mackasey (Parliamentary Secretary of Minister of Labour):,Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour,HOUSING-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN BUILDING RECREATIONAL FACILITIES,,,Mr. Speaker, because of the absence of the minister, who I am sure would have replied much more adequately than I, it is my duty to respond to the eloquent plea of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway urging the inclusion of recreational facilities in public housing. The fact that the hon. member has contacted the minister, the fact that the mayor and certain aldermen of the city of Vancouver travelled to Ottawa on October 5 to plead their case, and the fact that Bill No. C-241 will soon come before the house all show that the minister is fully aware of the arguments made on behalf of recreational fac lities. I do not think there is anybody in the house who would disagree with the argument of the hon. member that recreational facilities are needed, particularly in this type of housing project.

However, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member will agree with me that it is not clear who has the responsibility for providing these facilities. Obviously nothing in the present housing act permits the federal government to assume jurisdiction in this area. I think it is encouraging to a federalist to know that the civic authorities are quite willing to share in the financial burden of this type of project not only with the federal government but the provincial government. I would be interested in knowing whether the provincial government agrees with the suggestion that they absorb one-third of the cost of such projects, as originally put forward by the civic authorities.

The hon. member and others will have an opportunity when Bill No. C-241 is before the house in the very near future to suggest this very worth-while amendment and the minister will probably give his reasons for opposition to or agreement with the arguments presented. It may be unconstitutional for the federal government to do this; I have no way of knowing that. But I assure the hon. member that she will have an opportunity in a matter of weeks to place this suggestion more fully before the house.

Keays (Gaspe):,,HOUSING-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN BUILDING RECREATIONAL FACILITIES,,,Mr. Speaker, the problem I am about to raise is one that on three occasions already I have put before the minister and the house. It requires a very simple answer. My question is: What is happening to the fisheries office which is now in Gaspe? This office answers all the problems of the fishermen of the province of Quebec. They are not local problems but provincial problems and therefore that much more important. On three previous occasions I have asked for information on this subject and to date have not received an answer.

As the parliamentary secretary possibly knows, there are at the Gaspe office five employees who work under the fisheries indemnity plan. There are also seven or perhaps eight field officers who in some cases do the work called for under the fisheries indemnity plan and in other cases combine inspection service work and work under this plan.

I consider this problem important enough to raise during the adjournment debate because of the type of work that is carried out by the officers and those who administer the office. First of all, they administer the fisheries indemnity plan. They also deal with problems raised with regard to the insurance of fishing vessels. Further, they deal with the insurance of lobster traps, and more recently with the insurance of fixed gear. Beyond all this they administer the salt assistance plan of the Department of Fisheries. These things alone justify the office of the Department of Fisheries being in the area where the fisheries industry exists. You will not find any fishermen around the city of Quebec; you will not find them on the St. Charles River or the Red River. You will find them on the lower St. Lawrence, and the central point is the Gaspe area.

These employees have to oversee the insurance of 1,600 to 1,700 fishing vessels. This alone demonstrates the importance of the industry to the lower St. Lawrence. These fishermen are all quite close to the Gaspe area and need to have personal contact with officers of the Department of Fisheries. I hope hon. members realize that our fishermen are not white-collar executives. They spend a great deal of their time at sea, and conditions do not permit their using a typewriter when sailing over the rough waters of the St. Lawrence. When they are home on Sundays they do not require their wives to sit down

column2: COMMONS

column1: Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and write letters to the departmental officials.
I think the department owes them personal contact; the fisheries officials should meet the fishermen to hear their problems and to do something about them.

I will give a recent example of what happened in a small fishing village in my riding. A fisherman who had insured his boat under the fisheries indemnity plan saw it subsequently destroyed in a storm. The boat could not be used any longer so he brought it up on the shore and dismantled it. When the fisheries officer came to inspect the boat, it was gone. Many witnesses saw the boat, but the fisherman who is claiming insurance cannot produce proof of his loss. This is not due to any operations of a genius. He is a simple fisherman who said to himself: Since my boat is no longer worth anything, I will break it up and use it to kindle my fire. Nevertheless he had invested possibly $500 in that boat. He owes money to the bank but unfortunately he is not able to produce proof of the loss. How can he justify his claim?

There are officers working in the area but should the administrative office be moved back to the city they will still have to communicate with the fishermen. By the time they get to the fishermen there will be many more such problems. This situation is similar to what has happened with the closing of certain Unemployment Insurance Commission offices. You are putting the administration on wheels and the only people you are going to help are service station attendants and hotelkeepers. There will be more inspectors on the highway but this will not improve the service to the fisherman because by the time it reaches him it will be too late.

There are many other reasons I could bring forward but I will not take up the full time allotted to me. Fishermen in that area would like the administrative officers to be present in their area instead of being located in Quebec city. I hope we will realize the needs of the fishermen and will not revert to the situation which has existed in the past.

2446008,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.27.1,1966-11-07,9c7dcb09-291d-46ff-a24a-1e789d090b21,ca.m.7395,Mr. Milton L. Klein (Cartier):,,"EXPO '67-MONTREAL, P.Q., SUGGESTED IMPOSITION OF RENT CONTROLS",,,"Mr. Speaker, last week I directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in which I asked him whether the government would consider imposing the necessary measures to freeze leases and to establish rent controls on all dwellings and housing accommodation in the city of Montreal within a radius of 60 miles until May 1, 1968, when the abnormal accommodation problem created by Expo would have subsided. I think that the reason for this question is obvious. Up till now the emphasis has been on protecting visitors who will be coming to Expo. However, I believe the citizens of Montreal equally require the protection of the law with respect to their right to the accommodation they now occupy.
November 7, 19G6
column2: COMMONS

column1: The statistics projected by the Expo authorities indicate that, considering the number of people who will come to Montreal during Expo, accommodation will be required for these vast numbers not only in the city of Montreal but also in an area extending to Ottawa, St. Jovite, Three Rivers, Cornwall and down to the United States border. If this is true, and I have no doubt that it is, it indicates that the existing accommodation within the immediate vicinity of Expo and the island of Montreal itself will become premium accommodation. It will be very tempting to landlords who now own property in the city of Montreal to lease it out on a nightly basis rather than to keep their tenants who were with them previously in the property on a yearly basis.

I believe it is unrealistic to think that somebody who wanted to visit Expo for two or three days during one week would room in Ottawa, travel to Montreal, visit Expo, come back to Ottawa at night to sleep, then return to Montreal the next day to visit Expo, and do this two or three times during the week. During the operation of the world's fair in New York the state of New York imposed rent control and the situation was handled adequately as a result. Furthermore, the world's fair took place during the period May 1 to October 1 when the tourist trade in New York city is at its lowest ebb. The reverse is the case in Montreal. From the period May 1, 1967 to October 1, 1967, when Expo will be in operation, the tourist trade is at its highest level, and accommodation raises some problem even when Expo is not a factor as it will be in 1967.

My feeling is that Expo is a national undertaking. Because of this the situation that has been created is in fact of national interest. It seems to me that the government ought to provide stand-by legislation which need not necessarily be put into effect immediately but can be implemented if the situation gets out of hand. This legislation should be retroactive to November 1, 1966.

It may be that all parties in the house would consent to putting through such standby legislation rapidly. I point out that the machinery required to operate this legislation is in effect in the Montreal area at the present time. There is rent control, but in my view it is not adequate to cope with the situation that I believe will arise probably by February 1, 1967. Many tenants may not even be aware that when their leases expire on May 1, 1967, under certain circumstances 23033-6111
DEBATES

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion they are not even entitled to notice but may be told that they must vacate. This, I submit, will create great hardship in Montreal and will place many of our citizens in a difficult position. The last thing we want to do in our centennial year, I should think, is to place large numbers of our citizens in positions of hardship in Montreal during the term of Expo. I urge that in the interests of the citizens of Montreal steps be taken to control this situation.

,Liberal,,Milton L. Klein,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=9c7dcb09-291d-46ff-a24a-1e789d090b21&Language=E&Section=ALL
2446009,ca.proc.d.1966-11-07.27.2,1966-11-07,intervention,,,,EXPO '67-MONTREAL, P.Q., SUGGESTED IMPOSITION OF RENT CONTROLS",,,"Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the minister who is present in the house I am pleased to assure my hon. friend that the government of Canada, the government of Quebec, the city of Montreal and the Expo Corporation are fully aware of the importance of making good accommodation available efficiently and at reasonable rates to the millions of visitors expected at Expo '67.

The corporation has set up a reservations department called Logexpo which has already made 90,000 reservations covering some 370,000 hotel days or bed nights as the experts in Montreal call them. Logexpo is in a position to make reservations at reasonable prices for all inquirers at the present time. In this work the organization is receiving full co-operation from the Quebec Hotel Owners' Association, the government of the province of Quebec and, indeed, from a number of agencies in parts of eastern Ontario within easy driving distance of the exhibition site.

Hon. members will be aware that any legislative action that may be required is in the hands of the province of Quebec. In this respect the Prime Minister of Quebec has indicated on a number of occasions in recent weeks that the province is fully aware of its responsibilities as the host province during Expo and will take all measures necessary to ensure that visitors are well received and fairly treated. This legislative action might also include the protection of tenants now living in Montreal. We feel that the government's hands are tied. This is a provincial responsibility. The federal government can act only on a national basis and under certain circumstances.

All of us associated with the exhibition are keeping the closest continuing watch on the accommodation situation in Montreal. It is our hope that common sense and good citizenship will prevail and, indeed, they are prevailing up until the present time. Any
November 7, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion excesses or abuses can be expected from only a very small minority and will be dealt with firmly as they arise. The international reputation of Montreal, Quebec and, indeed, the entire country is at stake in this exhibition, as are the future prospects for our tourist industry. Expo '67 is a great business opportunity for Canada and we do not intend to permit a very few people to jeopardize its success.
